Regularization and embedded importance

Source: vignettes/articles/regularization.Rmd
regularization.Rmd

The four functions on this page each fit one model and read the selection off that model’s structure. fs_lasso() and fs_elastic() keep the predictors whose penalized coefficients are not zero, fs_randomforest() ranks predictors by permutation importance, and fs_mars() keeps the predictors that appear in its pruned spline terms. Because every predictor is in the model at once, each one is judged in the presence of the others, which a univariate filter cannot do.

fs_lasso() and fs_elastic() fit linear models, so they miss a predictor whose effect is curved, and neither holds out any rows, so neither gives you an honest performance estimate. fs_randomforest() and fs_mars() pick up non-linear effects, and both report metrics on a held-out split that the selection never saw.

For which quantities are honest and which are optimistic across all of featR, see Validation and leakage. For help choosing between these and the filter or wrapper methods, see Choosing a method.

Example data

Every example below uses the same simulated regression problem, so you can check each method against the known answer. y depends on x1, x2 and x3 linearly and on x_nl through a U-shaped curve with almost no linear trend. x1_copy is x1 plus a little noise, and x4 to x10 are pure noise.

set.seed(11)
n <- 300
d <- as.data.frame(matrix(rnorm(n * 10), n, 10,
                          dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("x", 1:10))))
d$x1_copy <- d$x1 + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)
d$x_nl    <- runif(n, -2, 2)
d$y <- 2 * d$x1 - 1.5 * d$x2 + 0.75 * d$x3 + 1.5 * (d$x_nl^2 - 4 / 3) + rnorm(n)

fs_lasso()

The lasso is linear regression with an L1 penalty on the coefficients. The penalty shrinks coefficients toward zero and sets some of them exactly to zero, and the predictors left with a non-zero coefficient are the selection. fs_lasso() fits it with glmnet::cv.glmnet(), choosing the penalty strength by cross-validation (nfolds = 5 by default). It handles numeric outcomes only (gaussian family); for classification, use fs_elastic().

las <- fs_lasso(d, "y", nfolds = 5, seed = 1)
las
#> <fs_result> lasso (regression)
#> Selected 8 of 12 features
#>   x2, x1, x1_copy, x3, x_nl, x4, x5, x9
#> Details: lambda_min, lambda_1se, lambda_used, coefficients, n_features (in $details)
head(las$scores, 6)
#>   Variable Coefficient AbsCoefficient
#> 1       x2  -1.4237946      1.4237946
#> 2       x1   1.0857606      1.0857606
#> 3  x1_copy   0.7641129      0.7641129
#> 4       x3   0.6011092      0.6011092
#> 5     x_nl   0.2535626      0.2535626
#> 6       x4   0.0425803      0.0425803

The lasso kept 8 of the 12 predictors: the four real ones, x1_copy, and three noise columns (x4, x5, x9). The default, lambda = "min", selects at the penalty that minimizes cross-validated error. That penalty is tuned for prediction, and it usually lets some noise through. lambda = "1se" uses the largest penalty whose error is within one standard error of the minimum, which gives a sparser and more stable set. On this data it drops the three noise columns:

selected(fs_lasso(d, "y", nfolds = 5, seed = 1, lambda = "1se"))
#> [1] "x2"      "x1"      "x1_copy" "x3"      "x_nl"

Both penalty values are stored in details$lambda_min and details$lambda_1se, whichever one you select at.

scores holds each coefficient multiplied by its column’s standard deviation, so predictors measured in different units can be ranked against each other. The raw coefficients are in details$coefficients. With standardize = FALSE the two tables are identical, and you should compare them only across predictors that share a scale.

Read the selection with three limits in mind:

  • Among strongly correlated predictors, the lasso tends to keep one and zero out the rest, so a missing predictor is not evidence that it is unrelated to the outcome. Here x1 and x1_copy both survive, but they split one effect between them (scores 1.09 and 0.76, which together come close to the true coefficient of 2), so neither coefficient measures it alone.
  • The model is linear. x_nl has one of the strongest effects in the data, but its score is 0.25 against 1.42 for x2, coming only from whatever linear trend this sample happens to contain. Compare the random forest and MARS results below.
  • fs_lasso() reports no performance estimate. If you keep the fitted model (return_model = TRUE), its cross-validated error is the one the penalty was chosen to minimize, so it is optimistic.

Factors and character columns are expanded into dummy columns, and the selection names those columns (colorred, not color). A factor with fewer than two observed levels is an error, and so is a dummy name that collides with another column (factor g with level b next to a column called gb). Infinite values are an error too.

Missing predictor values are an error under the default impute = "none". impute = "mean" fills them with column means computed on the whole data set, before cross-validation, so the folds see each other; featR warns when you use it. If you need imputation, do it inside your own resampling loop.

alpha defaults to 1. A value between 0 and 1 gives an elastic-net penalty at that fixed mixing value; fs_elastic() tunes it for you instead.

fs_elastic()

The elastic net mixes the lasso’s L1 penalty with the L2 (ridge) penalty. The mixing parameter alpha runs from 0 (pure ridge) to 1 (pure lasso). fs_elastic() tunes alpha and the penalty strength lambda together by resampling, through caret::train(method = "glmnet"), with 5-fold cross-validation unless you pass your own trControl. Unlike fs_lasso(), it also handles classification.

el <- fs_elastic(d, "y", alpha_seq = c(0.25, 0.5, 1), seed = 1)
el$details$best_alpha
#> [1] 0.5
el$details$metric_value
#> [1] 2.110188
selected(el)
#>  [1] "x1"      "x2"      "x3"      "x4"      "x5"      "x7"      "x8"     
#>  [8] "x9"      "x1_copy" "x_nl"

The winning alpha was 0.5, and 10 of the 12 predictors survived, including five of the seven noise columns. When alpha is below 1, the ridge part of the penalty spreads weight across correlated predictors, so a group like x1 and x1_copy tends to stay in together rather than being cut to one representative. The cost, as here, is a less sparse selection.

The winner is the pair with the best resampled metric, and picking the best of many candidates leans toward too little penalty. On pure-noise data (100 rows, 50 predictors) the default selected 8.5 predictors on average and at least one in every run. Passing a caret::trainControl() with selectionFunction = "oneSE" picks the most penalized pair within one standard error of the best, which selected 1.8 on average in the same simulation.

The same optimism applies to details$metric_value, the resampled RMSE of the winning pair (2.11 here). It is the best value over the whole grid, and fs_elastic() holds out no test rows, so treat it as optimistic and wrap the whole call in an outer resampling loop if you need an honest estimate. In model$results, caret’s Rsquared is the squared correlation between predictions and observations, not 1 - SSE/SST.

The default alpha_seq is seq(0.1, 1, by = 0.1). It leaves out alpha = 0 because ridge never sets a coefficient exactly to zero; if you add 0 yourself and it wins, every predictor is “selected” and featR warns. scores are absolute coefficients on the scale of the columns as supplied (NULL for an outcome with more than two classes, where each predictor has one coefficient per class). fs_elastic() does not rescale them the way fs_lasso() does, so standardize the predictors first if you want to rank by scores.

Rows with a missing outcome or any missing predictor are dropped before fitting. Factors are expanded into k - 1 dummy columns, and the selection names those columns. With use_pca = TRUE (and nPCs set), the model is fit on principal components that are recomputed inside every resample, and the selection then names components (PC1, PC2, …) rather than your columns.

fs_randomforest()

A random forest averages many decision trees, each grown on a bootstrap sample with a random subset of predictors tried at each split. fs_randomforest() splits the data (train_ratio = 0.75 by default, set through control), grows the forest on the training rows, and reports permutation importance plus metrics on the held-out rows. Permutation importance measures how much the forest’s error grows when one predictor’s values are shuffled.

task defaults to "classification", because a numeric column can be a class label, so pass task = "regression" for a numeric outcome. featR warns when a numeric target meets the default.

rf <- fs_randomforest(d, "y", task = "regression",
                      control = list(ntree = 300), seed = 1)
head(rf$scores, 6)
#>        x2      x_nl        x1   x1_copy        x3        x7 
#> 26.187296 26.142210 18.069593 17.606422  4.794183  1.894942
rf$details$metrics
#> $RMSE
#> [1] 1.645803
#> 
#> $MAE
#> [1] 1.326286
#> 
#> $R2
#> [1] 0.770357

The forest ranks x_nl second, almost tied with x2, where the linear methods gave it a small coefficient. x1 and x1_copy split their shared credit (18.1 and 17.6), and the noise columns trail far behind, led by x7 at 1.9. These scores are the mean increase in MSE divided by its standard error over trees; set control$scale_importance = FALSE for the unscaled version. Importance can also favor predictors with many distinct values, so treat close scores as ties.

A forest ranks predictors without selecting any. Unless you supply a selection rule, selected is every predictor, ordered by importance. To turn the ranking into a selection, pass a function as control$feature_select. It receives the training rows as a data.table and returns the columns to keep, including the outcome. The hook below keeps a fixed list for illustration; a real rule would compute something from dt.

top5 <- function(dt) {
  keep <- c("x1", "x2", "x3", "x_nl", "x1_copy")  # any rule you like
  dt[, c(keep, "y"), with = FALSE]
}
rf_sel <- fs_randomforest(d, "y", task = "regression",
                          control = list(ntree = 300, feature_select = top5),
                          seed = 1)
selected(rf_sel)
#> [1] "x_nl"    "x2"      "x1"      "x1_copy" "x3"

The hook runs after the split and sees only the training rows, so the held-out details$metrics stay honest even when the rule looks at the outcome. The out-of-bag error in details$oob does not: the forest is grown on the same rows the hook just selected on, so after a hook that consults the outcome the OOB error is optimistic. control$preprocess, by contrast, runs on the full data before the split, so keep it to row-wise transformations.

Missing predictor values are imputed by default with the median (numeric) or most common value (other types), learned on the training rows only. Rows with a missing outcome are dropped with a warning. With n_cores above 1 the forest is grown in pieces and combined, which discards the OOB results, so details$oob is NULL.

fs_mars()

MARS (multivariate adaptive regression splines) builds a model from piecewise-linear hinge functions, adding terms greedily and then pruning them back. It finds curved effects and, with degree above 1, interactions on its own. fs_mars() fits it with the earth package through caret, tunes degree and nprune (the number of terms kept) by repeated cross-validation, evaluates on a held-out split (train_ratio = 0.8), and selects the predictors that appear in the pruned model. The task follows the outcome: numeric means regression, factor or character means classification.

The defaults tune degree = 1:3 with 5-fold cross-validation repeated 3 times. The example uses a smaller grid to keep it fast.

ma <- fs_mars(d, "y", degree = 1:2, nprune = c(5, 10, 15),
              number = 3, repeats = 1, seed = 1)
selected(ma)
#> [1] "x1_copy" "x_nl"    "x2"      "x3"
ma$details$metrics
#> $RMSE
#> [1] 0.9944926
#> 
#> $MAE
#> [1] 0.8114338
#> 
#> $R2
#> [1] 0.9184193
ma$details$removed_predictors
#> $nzv
#> character(0)
#> 
#> $corr
#> [1] "x1"

MARS found x_nl along with x2, x3 and x1_copy, and kept none of the noise columns. x1 is missing because of a filter that runs before the model is fit. fs_mars() drops near-zero-variance predictors and one member of each pair correlated above corr_cut (default 0.95), and details$removed_predictors records what went. Both filters are fit on the training rows only, and neither looks at the outcome, so which of x1 and x1_copy survives says nothing about which matters more. Set corr_cut = 0 to turn the correlation filter off.

The reported R2 is caret’s squared correlation between predictions and observations, not 1 - SSE/SST, and a biased model can still score well on it, so read it together with RMSE. fs_randomforest() reports 1 - SSE/SST, so the two R2 values on this page are not comparable. RMSE is on the same scale for both (0.99 for MARS against 1.65 for the forest), but each comes from one split of a different size, so on small data treat the gap as rough.

Rows with any missing value are dropped before anything else, so fs_mars() needs fairly complete data. Data with more than sample_size rows (default 10000) are then randomly down-sampled to that size before the split.

For classification fs_mars() needs the e1071 package, and it up-samples the smaller classes inside each resample rather than before cross-validation. It treats the first factor level as the positive class for PR AUC, sensitivity and specificity, with no override, so use stats::relevel() to change it. fs_randomforest() uses the second level unless you set control$positive_class, so those class-specific numbers do not compare across the two functions (ROC AUC does). Test-set ROC and PR AUC are reported for binary outcomes when pROC and PRROC are installed.
